answer_text:
We interpret the question as asking for the **maximum** number of knights.

A knight move changes the color of a square, since it moves \(1+2=3\) squares total, an odd number. Therefore, any set of squares all of the same color is automatically safe: no two knights on that color attack each other.

---

## 1. The \(8\times 8\) board

An \(8\times 8\) board has 32 black squares and 32 white squares. Placing a knight on every square of one color gives

\[
32
\]

non-attacking knights.

To show we cannot do better, partition the board into eight \(2\times 4\) rectangles. In each \(2\times 4\) rectangle, pair the squares as follows:

\[
\begin{array}{cccc}
A & B & C & D\\
C & D & A & B
\end{array}
\]

Each identical letter marks two squares a knight’s move apart:
- \(A\) differs by \((1,2)\),
- \(B\) differs by \((1,2)\),
- \(C\) differs by \((1,2)\),
- \(D\) differs by \((1,2)\).

Thus each \(2\times 4\) block is split into 4 disjoint attacking pairs. Since the whole board contains 8 such blocks, it is split into

\[
8\cdot 4=32
\]

disjoint attacking pairs.

In any safe placement, we can place at most one knight on each attacking pair, so we can place at most 32 knights.

Since 32 knights are achievable, the maximum on an \(8\times 8\) board is

\[
32.
\]

---

## 2. The \(5\times 5\) board

A \(5\times 5\) board has 13 squares of one color and 12 of the other. Placing knights on all 13 squares of the larger color gives

\[
13
\]

non-attacking knights.

To show we cannot place 14, pair up 24 of the 25 squares into 12 disjoint attacking pairs, leaving one square unpaired. One such pairing is:

\[
\begin{array}{ccccc}
D & A & C & B & *\\
C & H & D & I & E\\
A & F & K & G & B\\
H & L & I & E & J\\
F & K & J & L & G
\end{array}
\]

Each identical letter marks two squares a knight’s move apart, and \(*\) is the single unpaired square. For example:
- \(A\) is at \((1,2)\) and \((3,1)\),
- \(B\) is at \((1,4)\) and \((3,5)\),
- \(C\) is at \((1,3)\) and \((2,1)\),
- and similarly for the others.

There are 12 attacking pairs plus 1 unpaired square. A safe placement can use at most one square from each pair, and at most one square total from the singleton, so the total is at most

\[
12+1=13.
\]

Since 13 knights are achievable, the maximum on a \(5\times 5\) board is

\[
13.
\]

---

Therefore, the maximum numbers are

\[
\boxed{32\text{ on an }8\times8\text{ board, and }13\text{ on a }5\times5\text{ board}}
\]
